content: Jing, in the context of Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), refers to the concept of essence, specifically the kidney essence. Jing is stored in the kidneys and represents the densest physical substance within the body, in contrast to shen, which is considered the most ethereal or volatile. Jing serves as the material foundation of the physical body and is classified as yin in nature, meaning it has nourishing, cooling, and sustaining properties. This makes it a critical concept not only in TCM but also in internal martial arts practices. Jing is thought to carry hereditary information, drawing a parallel to the modern understanding of DNA. In men, the production of semen, and in women, the production of menstrual blood or the process of pregnancy, are believed to place significant demands on jing. However, equating jing solely with semen is an oversimplification. Jing circulates through the eight extraordinary vessels in the body and contributes to the formation of marrow, semen, and other essential substances. It is believed that individuals are born with a finite amount of jing, referred to as pre-natal jing or yuan qi. This pre-natal jing is inherited from one’s parents and cannot be replenished. Additionally, post-natal jing can be acquired through food, exercise, intellectual stimulation, and meditative practices. Throughout life, jing is continuously consumed by various factors, including stress, illness, substance abuse, and excessive sexual activity. The depletion of pre-natal jing is considered irreversible, and it is said to be completely exhausted at the time of death. Therefore, preserving jing is regarded as essential for health and longevity in TCM. Practices such as qigong, internal martial arts (e.g., Tai Chi Chuan), and Baguazhang’s Circle Walking are believed to help conserve pre-natal jing and replenish post-natal jing when performed correctly. In Chinese herbal medicine, certain remedies are thought to support jing. For example, ginseng (rénshēn), particularly Korean and Chinese varieties, is commonly used to strengthen jing. A traditional recipe involves adding ginseng, cinnamon, goji berries, and ginger to porridge (congee) to create a warming and nourishing breakfast, especially during the colder months of autumn. The concept of jing has deep historical roots, with one of its earliest mentions found in the 4th century BCE text Inner Training (內業), a chapter of the Guanzi (管子), compiled during the Han dynasty. It is important to distinguish jing (精; essence) from other related terms, such as jin (勁; power) and jing (經; classic/warp), the latter of which appears in the titles of many classical Chinese texts, such as the Nei Jing (Inner Classic), Yi Jing (Book of Changes), and Cha Jing (Classic of Tea). Interestingly, the concept of jing has also been referenced in modern popular culture, such as in the animated series Avatar: The Last Airbender.
